reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that modern football’s shift toward quantification enables structured analysis of player development through tracking data. Path similarity captures behavioral consistency in pass blocking, while expected depth provides a scalar measure of positional effectiveness. Development efficiency ties these metrics to economic incentives, suggesting that tools must account for both performance gains and cost-benefit ratios. These primitives form a dual structure: one rooted in kinematic behavior (path similarity), another in strategic outcome (expected depth), both grounded in empirical observables. Failure modes arise from noisy data, insufficient temporal resolution, or misalignment between training and game contexts. Dualities emerge between individual skill and systemic impact—where a single poor block can derail an entire play, yet repeated small improvements compound into significant gains. The framework assumes stationarity in player behavior and feature independence, which may fail under dynamic or chaotic game states.
